Rakesh Singh Jadon vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6
December, 2024
Author: Gurpal Singh Ahluwalia 
Bench: G. S. Ahluwalia
 Neutral Citation No. 2024:Mphc-Gwl:22396
 1 
 In The High Court Of Madhya Pradesh
 At G Wa L I O R
 Before
 Hon'Ble Shri Justice G. S. Ahluwalia
 On The 6th Of December, 2024
 Misc. Criminal Case No. 325 of 2023
 Rakesh Singh Jadon And Others
 Versus
 The State Of Madhya Pradesh And Others
 Appearance:
 Shri J.S. Rathore- Advocate for applicants.
 Shri Naval Kishor Gupta- Public Prosecutor for responden
 Shri Shiv Kumar Yadav - Advocate for respondent No.2.
 Order
This application, under Section 482 of Cr.P.C., has been filed for quashment of FIR in Crime No.187/2022 registered at Police Station Mahila Thana, District Gwalior (M.P.) for offences punishable under Sections 498-A, 506, 34 of IPC and under Sections 3 and 4 of Dowry Prohibition Act as well as consequential proceedings arising out of it. 
2. Undisputed facts are that applicant No.1 is the husband, applicants No.2 and 3 are father-in-law and mother-in-law and applicant No.4 is the elder brother- in-law (tsB) of respondent No.2.
3. Prosecution story, in short, is that respondent No.2 lodged an FIR on 30.06.2022 alleging inter alia that she got married to applicant No.1 on NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-GWL:22396 11.07.2013 in accordance with Hindu rites and rituals. Her parents had given cash amount of Rakesh Singh Jadon vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80160059/ 
1 Rs.Seven Lacs, household articles and gold & silver ornaments. In all, a total amount of Rs.15 lacs was spent in the marriage. When she went to her matrimonial house, then she was kept properly by applicants for some time and thereafter, applicants started harassing her on the question of giving less dowry and they used to allege that her parents had not given sufficient dowry as per the demand and thus they started demanding an amount of Rs.Five Lacs as well as a motorcycle. When she refused to fulfill their demands then they used to beat her physically and harass her mentally. 
However, under hope and belief that with passage of time, things would improve, she was tolerating the same. However, behaviour of applicants did not change and on account of non-fulfillment of demand of Rs.Five Lacs and a motorcycle they turned her out of her matrimonial house with a specific direction that she should not come back without motorcyle and cash of Rs.Five Lacs and in case she tries to come back then she would be killed. She went to her parental home and informed the entire incident to her parents. Thereafter, applicants came to her parental home and again demanded the amount of Rs.Five Lacs and a motorcycle and extended her threat that unless and until their demands are fulfilled, complainant should not be sent back to her matrimonial house. 
Her parents made every possible effort to convince and persuade applicants but they did not agree and accordingly, FIR was lodged.
4 . Challenging the aforesaid FIR, it is submitted by counsel for applicants that applicant No.1 has filed a petition for divorce on 15.12.2021 and only after receiving notice of the same, FIR in question was lodged on 30.06.2022. Furthermore, during counselling applicant No.1 had filed an application on 30.06.2022 thereby complaining misbehaviour of respondent No.2 as well as false allegations made by her on account of institution of petition for divorce. 
NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-GWL:22396 Applicant No.4 had made a complaint to Superintendent of Police, Gwalior, seeking free and fair investigation into the allegations made against him. It is the case of applicants that applicant No.4 is residing separately at Sankatmochan Nagar, Suraiyapura, Morar, District Gwalior and his children are getting education in different schools in Gwalior. Applicant No.4 had already shifted to Gwalior sometime in the year 2009. He is in a private job and is not residing with applicants No.1 to 3 since 2009. 
5. The police has filed charge-sheet against all applicants in RCT No.4396/2022 which is pending. 
6. IA. No.11175/2023 has been filed by applicants with a prayer to take documents on record. Along with this application, proceedings of reconciliation which took place on 13.06.2022 have been placed on record, according to which applicant No.4 had appeared on behalf of applicants No.1 to 3 for reconciliation purposes. 
7. Per contra, application is vehemently opposed by counsel for State as well as counsel for respondent No.2. It is submitted that it is quite clear from the reconciliation proceedings relied upon by applicants themselves that applicant No.4 was representing applicants No.1 to 3, therefore,
it cannot be said that he had nothing to say in the family affairs of applicants No.1 to 3. There is a specific allegation that all four applicants went to the house of complainant at Gwalior and extended threat after making demand of Rs.Five Lacs and a motorcycle. 
Rakesh Singh Jadon vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80160059/
2 8. Considered the submissions made by counsel for the parties. 
9. The FIR which was lodged by complainant has already been reproduced. 
Applicant No.4- Raghvendra Singh Jadon: 
10. Applicant No.4 is elder-brother-law (Jeth) of respondent No.2 and according to this applicant he i s r e s i d i n g i n G w a l i o r w h e r e a s t h e m a t r i m o n i a l N E U T R A L C I T A T I O N N O .
2024:MPHC-GWL:22396 house of respondent No.2 is situated in Sabalgarh, District Morena and applicants No.1 to 3 are residents of "behind Sudamapuri Girls School, Police Station and Tahsil Sabalgarh, District Morena (M.P.)". In order to prosecute the near and dear relatives of husband,
allegations must be specific and clear and they should not be omnibus and general in nature. 
Although applicant No.4 has claimed that he is the resident of Sankatmochan Nagar, Suraiyapura,
Morar, District Gwalior but the parental home of respondent No.2 is also situated at Randheer Singh Colony, Gola Ka Mandir, Gwalior. In the FIR, it was specifically alleged by complainant/respondent No.2 that all applicants including applicant No.4 came to her parental home at Gwalior and again demanded an amount of Rs.Five Lacs and a motorcycle with clear threat that otherwise they would not keep the complainant with them and also extended threat to her life. 
Since applicant No.4 is the resident of Gwalior and allegations are that he had visited the parental home of respondent No.2 along with other co-accused persons, it is clear that separate residence of applicant No.4 may not be a vital circumstance to suspect his false implication. Furthermore,
applicants themselves have filed IA.No.11175/2023 seeking permission to file documents on record. 
Along with the said application, reconciliation proceedings dated 13.06.2022 have been placed on record. From the said proceedings, it is clear that applicant No.4 had appeared as representative of applicants No.1 to 3. Since applicant No.1 was not present, therefore, the case was fixed for 30.06.2022. The reconciliation proceeding dated 13.06.2022 was also signed by applicant No.4. On 30.06.2022 also, applicant No.4 appeared along with applicant No.1. The presence of applicant No.4 has been specifically mentioned in the proceeding dated 30.06.2022 and the aforesaid proceedings are also signed by applicant No.4. In the proceedings dated 30.06.2022, it was specifically alleged by complainant that she is being harassed by her husband and NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2024:MPHC-GWL:22396 her in-laws and therefore she wants that she should be kept properly whereas applicant No.1 had expressed that since he has already instituted a suit for divorce therefore he does not wish to keep complainant with him. Thus, it is clear that applicant No.4 was actively representing applicants No.1 to 3 in the reconciliation proceedings. Allegations, made in the FIR to the effect that applicant No.4 had also visited the house of parents of respondent No.2 along with applicants No.1 to 3, demanded Rs.Five Lacs and a motorcycle and also extended threat that in case if demand is not fulfilled then they would not keep the complainant in matrimonial house,
appear to be prima facie correct. Under these circumstances, it is clear that there are clear and specific allegation against applicant No.4 with regard to harassment of respondent No.2 physically and mentally. Furthermore, compelling a married woman to live in her parental home on account of non- fulfillment of demand for dowry amounts to continuous act of cruelty. 
The Supreme Court in the case of Rupali Devi v. State of U.P., reported in (2019) 5 SCC 384 has held as under:-
Rakesh Singh Jadon vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80160059/
3 "14. "Cruelty" which is the crux of the offence under Section 498-A IPC is defined in Black's Law Dictionary to mean "the intentional and malicious infliction of mental or physical suffering on a living creature, esp. a human; abusive treatment; outrage (abuse, inhuman treatment, indignity)". Cruelty can be both physical or mental cruelty. The impact on the mental health of the wife by overt acts on the part of the husband or his relatives; the mental stress and trauma of being driven away from the matrimonial home and her helplessness to go back to the same home for fear of being ill-treated are aspects that cannot be ignored while understanding the meaning of the expression "cruelty" appearing in Section 498-A of the Penal Code. The emotional distress or psychological effect on the wife, if not the physical injury, is bound to continue to traumatise the wife even after she leaves the matrimonial home and takes shelter at the parental home. Even if the acts of physical cruelty committed in the matrimonial house may have ceased and such acts do not occur at the parental home,
there can be no doubt that the mental trauma and the psychological distress caused by the acts NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-GWL:22396 of the husband including verbal exchanges, if any, that had compelled the wife to leave the matrimonial home and take shelter with her parents would continue to persist at the parental home. Mental cruelty borne out of physical cruelty or abusive and humiliating verbal exchanges would continue in the parental home even though there may not be any overt act of physical cruelty at such place." 
This Court in the case of Amar Singh vs. Smt. Vimla decided on 22.06.2021 in Criminal Revision No.2376/2020 (Gwalior Bench) has held that compelling a married woman to live in her parental home amounts to cruelty. 
Thus, if applicant No.4 had insisted that unless and until demand is fulfilled respondent No.2/complainant should reside in her parental home, then it is clear that he is also prima facie guilty of committing cruelty and harassment on respondent No.2. 
Applicants No.2 and 3- Hawaldar Singh & Smt. Munni Devi: 
11. Allegations made against applicants No.2 and 3 have already been reproduced. 
Supreme Court in the case of Taramani Parakh Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh and Others reported in (2015) 11 SCC 260 has held as under:-
"12. In Kailash Chandra Agrawal v. State of U.P. (2014) 16 SCC 551, it was observed (SCC p. 553, paras 8-9):
"8. We have gone through the FIR and the criminal complaint. In the FIR, the appellants have not been named and in the criminal complaint they have been named without attributing any specific role to them. The relationship of the appellants with the husband of the complainant is distant. In Kans Raj v. State of Punjab (2000) 5 SCC 207 : 2000 SCC (Cri) 935 : (2000) 3 SCR 662]it was observed (SCC p. 217, para 5):
Rakesh Singh Jadon vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80160059/
4 "5. ... A tendency has, however, developed for roping in all relations of the in-laws of the deceased wives in the matters of dowry deaths which, if not discouraged, is likely to affect the case of the prosecution even against the real culprits. In their overenthusiasm and anxiety to NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-GWL:22396 seek conviction for maximum people, the parents of the deceased have been found to be making efforts for involving other relations which ultimately weaken the case of the prosecution even against the real accused as appears to have happened in the instant case." 
The Court has, thus, to be careful in summoning distant relatives without there being specific material. Only the husband, his parents or at best close family members may be expected to demand dowry or to harass the wife but not distant relations, unless there is tangible material to support allegations made against such distant relations. Mere naming of distant relations is not enough to summon them in the absence of any specific role and material to support such role. 
9. The parameters for quashing proceedings in a criminal complaint are well known. If there are triable issues, the Court is not expected to go into the veracity of the rival versions but where on the face of it, the criminal proceedings are abuse of Court's process, quashing jurisdiction can be exercised. Reference may be made to K. Ramakrishna v. State of Bihar, (2000) 8 SCC 547 : 2001 SCC (Cri) 27, Pepsi Foods Ltd. v.
Judicial Magistrate, (1998) 5 SCC 749 : 1998 SCC (Cri) 1400, State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335 : 1992 SCC (Cri) 426 : AIR 1992 SC 604 and Asmathunnisa v. State of A.P., (2011)
11 SCC 259 : (2011) 3 SCC (Cri) 159."
13. In the present case, the complaint is as follows:
"Sir, it is submitted that I was married on 18- 11-2009 with Sidharath Parakh s/o Manak Chand Parakh r/o Sarafa Bazar in front of Radha Krishna Market, Gwalior according to the Hindu rites and customs. In the marriage my father had given gold and silver ornaments, cash amount and household goods according to his capacity. 
After the marriage when I went to my matrimonial home, I was treated nicely by the members of the family. When on the second occasion I went to my matrimonial home, my husband, father-in-law and mother-in-law started harassing me for not bringing the dowry and started saying that NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2024:MPHC-GWL:22396 I should bring from my father 25-30 tolas of gold and Rs 2,00,000 in cash and only then they would keep me in the house otherwise not. On account of this my husband also used to beat me and my father-in-law and my mother-in-law used to torture me by giving the taunts. In this connection I used to tell my father Kundanmal Oswal, my mother Smt Prem Lata Oswal, uncle Ashok Rai Sharma and uncle Ved Prakash Mishra from time to time. On 2-4-2010 the members of the family of my matrimonial home forcibly sent me to the house of my parents in Ganj Basoda along with my brother Deepak. They snatched my clothes and ornaments and kept with them. Since then till today my husband has been harassing Rakesh Singh Jadon vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80160059/
5 me on the telephone and has not come to take me back. Being compelled, I have been moving this application before you. Sir, it is prayed that action be taken against husband Sidharath Parakh, my fatherin-law Manak Chand Parakh and my motherin-law Smt Indira Parakh for torturing me on account of demanding dowry. 
14. From a reading of the complaint, it cannot be held that even if the allegations are taken as proved no case is made out. There are allegations against Respondent 2 and his parents for harassing the complainant which forced her to leave the matrimonial home. Even now she continues to be separated from the matrimonial home as she apprehends lack of security and safety and proper environment in the matrimonial home. The question whether the appellant has in fact been harassed and treated with cruelty is a matter of trial but at this stage, it cannot be said that no case is made out. Thus, quashing of proceedings before the trial is not permissible." 
There are specific allegations of harassment, beating on account of non- fulfillment of demand of dowry of Rs.Five Lacs and a motorcycle. Furthermore, complainant/respondent No.2 has specifically alleged in her FIR that she was ousted by applicants from her matrimonial house on account of non-fulfillment of demand of dowry. Although the date of her ouster has not been mentioned in the FIR but it is clear from the divorce petition filed by applicant No.1 in which it is mentioned that respondent No.2/complainant had gone to the parental home on NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-GWL:22396 22.07.2021. Therefore, it is clear that complainant was ousted from her matrimonial house on 22.07.2021 and since then she is residing in her parental home. Considering the allegations made against applicants No.2 and 3 as well as in the light of judgment rendered by Supreme Court in the case of Taramani Parakh (supra), this Court is of the considered opinion that there is sufficient material against applicants No.2 and 3 to prosecute them for offences punishable under Sections 498A, 506, 34 of IPC and under Sections 3 and 4 of Dowry Prohibition Act. 
Applicant No.1 - Rakesh Singh Jadon:
12. Apart from other defences, it is also alleged by counsel for applicants that applicant No.1 has already instituted a suit for grant of divorce on 15.12.2021 and only after receiving notice of the same, complainant had lodged FIR, therefore, the same has been lodged by way of counterblast to the divorce petition. 
The question is no more res integra. 
Supreme Court in the case of Pratibha v. Rameshwari Devi, reported in (2007) 12 SCC 369 has held as under:-
"14. From a plain reading of the findings arrived at by the High Court while quashing the FIR, it is apparent that the High Court had relied on extraneous considerations and acted beyond the allegations made in the FIR for quashing the same in exercise of its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code. We have already noted the illustrations enumerated in Bhajan Lal case [1992 Supp (1) SCC 335 : 1992 SCC (Cri)
Rakesh Singh Jadon vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80160059/
6 426] and from a careful reading of these illustrations, we are of the view that the allegations emerging from the FIR are not covered by any of the illustrations as noted hereinabove. For example, we may take up one of the findings of the High Court as noted hereinabove. 
The High Court has drawn an adverse inference on account of the FIR being lodged on 31-12-2001 while the appellant was forced out of the matrimonial home on 25-5-2001. 
15. In our view, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Court was not justified in drawing an adverse inference against the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-GWL:22396 appellant wife for lodging the FIR on 31-12- 2001 on the ground that she had left the matrimonial home at least six months before that. This is because, in our view, the High Court had failed to appreciate that the appellant and her family members were, during this period, making all possible efforts to enter into a settlement so that Respondent 2 husband would take her back to the matrimonial home. If any complaint was made during this period, there was every possibility of not entering into any settlement with Respondent 2 husband. 
16. It is pertinent to note that the complaint was filed only when all efforts to return to the matrimonial home had failed and Respondent 2 husband had filed a divorce petition under Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. That apart, in our view, filing of a divorce petition in a civil court cannot be a ground to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Code as it is well settled that criminal and civil proceedings are separate and independent and the pendency of a civil proceeding cannot bring to an end a criminal proceeding even if they arise out of the same set of facts. Such being the position, we are, therefore, of the view that the High Court while exercising its powers under Section 482 of the Code has gone beyond the allegations made in the FIR and has acted in excess of its jurisdiction and, therefore, the High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR by going beyond the allegations made in the FIR or by relying on extraneous considerations. 
22. For the reasons aforesaid, we are inclined to interfere with the order of the High Court and hold that the High Court in quashing the FIR in the exercise of its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code by relying on the investigation report and the findings made therein has acted beyond its jurisdiction. For the purpose of finding out the commission of a cognizable offence, the High Court was only required to look into the allegations made in the complaint or the FIR and to conclude whether a prima facie offence had been made out by the complainant in the FIR or the complaint or not." 
Thus, it is clear that findings recorded by a civil court are not binding on criminal court and vice versa. If the complainant /wife maintains silence under hope and belief that with passage of time her matrimonial life would improve and ultimately after realizing that situation has reached to a point of no return and her NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-GWL:22396 in-laws have initiated proceedings for divorce with bleak chances of reconciliation, then if she decides to make a report with regard to cruelty meted out to her, then it cannot be said that patience shown by wife was unwarranted or it was her weakness. 
Rakesh Singh Jadon vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80160059/
7 13. Under these circumstances, it cannot be said that FIR lodged by respondent No.2 is bad as the same was lodged after institution of divorce petition. No other argument is advanced by counsel for applicants. 
14. Considering the totality of facts and circumstances of the case, this Court is of the considered opinion that no case is made out warranting interference. Application fails and is hereby dismissed. 
(G.S. Ahluwalia) Judge pd Rakesh Singh Jadon vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80160059/

annotations.text: "Cruelty" which is the crux of the offence under Section 498-A IPC is defined in Black's Law Dictionary to mean "the intentional and malicious infliction of mental or physical suffering on a living creature, esp. a human; abusive treatment; outrage (abuse, inhuman treatment, indignity)".
Cruelty can be both physical or mental cruelty.

The impact on the mental health of the wife by overt acts on the part of the husband or his relatives; the mental stress and trauma of being driven away from the matrimonial home and her helplessness to go back to the same home for fear of being ill-treated are aspects that cannot be ignored while understanding the meaning of the expression "cruelty" appearing in Section 498-A of the Penal Code.

The emotional distress or psychological effect on the wife, if not the physical injury, is bound to continue to traumatise the wife even after she leaves the matrimonial home and takes shelter at the parental home.

Even if the acts of physical cruelty committed in the matrimonial house may have ceased and such acts do not occur at the parental home,
there can be no doubt that the mental trauma and the psychological distress caused by the acts NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-GWL:22396 of the husband including verbal exchanges, if any, that had compelled the wife to leave the matrimonial home and take shelter with her parents would continue to persist at the parental home.

Mental cruelty borne out of physical cruelty or abusive and humiliating verbal exchanges would continue in the parental home even though there may not be any overt act of physical cruelty at such place."

This Court in the case of Amar Singh vs. Smt. Vimla decided on 22.06.2021 in Criminal Revision No.2376/2020 (Gwalior Bench) has held that compelling a married woman to live in her parental home amounts to cruelty.

Thus, if applicant No.4 had insisted that unless and until demand is fulfilled respondent No.2/complainant should reside in her parental home, then it is clear that he is also prima facie guilty of committing cruelty and harassment on respondent No.2.

annotations.text: A tendency has, however, developed for roping in all relations of the in-laws of the deceased wives in the matters of dowry deaths which, if not discouraged, is likely to affect the case of the prosecution even against the real culprits.

The Court has, thus, to be careful in summoning distant relatives without there being specific material.

annotations.text: For example, we may take up one of the findings of the High Court as noted hereinabove.
The High Court has drawn an adverse inference on account of the FIR being lodged on 31-12-2001 while the appellant was forced out of the matrimonial home on 25-5-2001.

15. In our view, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Court was not justified in drawing an adverse inference against the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-GWL:22396 appellant wife for lodging the FIR on 31-12- 2001 on the ground that she had left the matrimonial home at least six months before that.

This is because, in our view, the High Court had failed to appreciate that the appellant and her family members were, during this period, making all possible efforts to enter into a settlement so that Respondent 2 husband would take her back to the matrimonial home.
If any complaint was made during this period, there was every possibility of not entering into any settlement with Respondent 2 husband.

16. It is pertinent to note that the complaint was filed only when all efforts to return to the matrimonial home had failed and Respondent 2 husband had filed a divorce petition under Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

That apart, in our view, filing of a divorce petition in a civil court cannot be a ground to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Code as it is well settled that criminal and civil proceedings are separate and independent and the pendency of a civil proceeding cannot bring to an end a criminal proceeding even if they arise out of the same set of facts.

Such being the position, we are, therefore, of the view that the High Court while exercising its powers under Section 482 of the Code has gone beyond the allegations made in the FIR and has acted in excess of its jurisdiction and, therefore, the High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR by going beyond the allegations made in the FIR or by relying on extraneous considerations.

22. For the reasons aforesaid, we are inclined to interfere with the order of the High Court and hold that the High Court in quashing the FIR in the exercise of its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code by relying on the investigation report and the findings made therein has acted beyond its jurisdiction.

For the purpose of finding out the commission of a cognizable offence, the High Court was only required to look into the allegations made in the complaint or the FIR and to conclude whether a prima facie offence had been made out by the complainant in the FIR or the complaint or not."
Thus, it is clear that findings recorded by a civil court are not binding on criminal court and vice versa.
